newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore moves to curb public housing speculation.
newsitem.headline: Singapore moves to curb public housing speculation.

text.p: New curbs on property speculation in Singapore public housing should make flats more available to first-time buyers but are unlikely to heavily affect prices, analysts said.

After weeks of waiting, the Singapore government last week announced a slew of measures to curb speculation in public housing which has enabled owners to reap profits of as much as Singapore $300,000 (US$210,000).

The new curbs announced by the Housing Development Board (HDB) come barely a month after the government tightened up its mortgage financing policy for HDB flats to ensure that buyers buy within their means.
The government said the latest measures were aimed at cutting the average waiting time for genuine first-time home buyers to three years from an average of four-and-a-half years.
The measures include imposing a waiting period of 10 years before an HDB owner can buy a second subsidised flat from the government and also separate queues for first- and second-time HDB buyers.
Analysts said these measures are part of a comprehensive policy to keep public housing available and affordable.
"The first-time buyer will find it much easier to get a flat but the net impact on prices will not be so significant," Lim Chung Chun, investment analyst with ING Barings, said.
He said it was difficult to ascertain the intentions of those who upgrade public housing flats, but that capital gains were an incentive.
Most upgraders use the profits from selling their HDB units to make the initial downpayment for a private home.
A new four-room flat bought directly from the HDB cost about S$120,000 but a comparable unit sold in the secondary market in 1996 was $239,000, a recent Jones Lang Wootton study showed.
About 90 percent of Singaporeans live in public housing and nearly all own their units.
HDB flat prices have risen sharply in recent years in tandem with the sharp rise in private property prices.
The queue to buy HDB flats has also surged with growing affluence along with the prospect of making good profits from owning such flats.
Figures show that early this year some 146,000 people were waiting to buy a unit from the government compared with 80,000 in 1994.
A lot of those in the queue are existing HDB homeowners who plan to sell their homes at a higher price on the secondary market and buy a new and cheaper unit from the government.
"There is an anomaly in housing allocation. The government has to weed out those who need it from those who want more," Steven Choo, executive director with Jones Lang Wootton said.
Choo said it was wise for the authorities to introduce discipline and order to the public housing market.
"Buying of HDB flats and upgrading (from smaller units to larger ones) is a cornerstone of the housing sector. Demand for public housing is inelastic," Choo said.
Some analysts also said the latest government measures would temper prices in the private home market.
Both markets are closely linked as most HDB homeowners aspire to upgrade to private homes.
US$1 = S$1.43 REUTER
